summary:
ARES (Astronaut Route & Exploration System) is an interactive 2D/3D web map for planning surface traverses on Mars. We built it for the Martian Map challenge: it layers real NASA data (MOLA elevation, Viking and CTX imagery) with estimated radiation dose and surface temperature, over two regions, Tharsis and Gale Crater. Users pick two sites and an A* search returns three routes (shortest, safest, lowest exposure), with slope, dose and temperature for each. A simplified solar-hour model shows when an EVA would be possible, and a simulated astronaut walks the route.

The challenge asks for a layered view that helps a human explorer plan a safe trip. ARES puts topography, imagery, radiation and temperature in one place and uses them to compare options.
details:
WHAT ARES DOES

ARES (Astronaut Route & Exploration System) is an interactive 2D/3D mission-planning map of Mars. It layers real NASA terrain and imagery with modelled radiation and temperature, and uses them to compute and compare walking routes between named sites in two regions: Tharsis (Pavonis, Arsia and Ascraeus Mons, Noctis Labyrinthus, western Valles Marineris) and Gale Crater (Bradbury Landing and Mount Sharp). Users fly over the terrain, pick two sites and get three routes, each with distance, slope, estimated dose and temperature, plus an EVA schedule and a simulated Marswalk.

HOW IT WORKS: KEY TECHNICAL INNOVATIONS

  1. Real terrain. Elevation comes from the MGS MOLA DEM exported from NASA Mars Trek: 1/16° cells (~3.7 km) for Tharsis and 1/128° (~463 m) for Gale. We also built a ~1 km inset from a Mars Trek OBJ export. After georeferencing it against MOLA (correlation 0.9999, median residual 1.2 m) we found it was MOLA resampled, so it adds a smoother mesh but no new topography.
  2. Three-profile A* routing. Shortest minimises 3D distance (steps over 25° forbidden). Safest multiplies distance by (1 + (slope/3°)²) and by a radiation and cold factor, with a 12° limit. Lowest exposure weights radiation and cold much more heavily, with a 15° limit. The heuristic never overestimates, so each route is optimal for its cost.
  3. Radiation model. Anchored to the MSL/RAD measurement at Gale (0.64 mSv/day) and scaled with the atmospheric column above each cell. It gives 0.63 to 0.98 mSv/day across our Tharsis terrain. GCR only.
  4. EVA windows. Surface temperature comes from the Mars Climate Database v6.2 (four seasons, 05:00 and 14:00 local time). A walk is allowed when the sun is between 5° and 60° above the horizon and the surface is at least 200 K. Pace is 3.5 km/h, slower on slopes. These are our demo thresholds, not NASA flight rules.
  5. Observed vs simulation. Every layer, site and route is tagged, so users always know what is data and what is a model.

HOW ARES ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asks for a layered view of a Martian location or route that combines data from several NASA missions. ARES combines five kinds of data: topographic (MGS MOLA), optical (Viking MDIM 2.1 and MRO CTX), thermal (THEMIS infrared mosaics and Mars Climate Database temperatures), geologic (USGS global geologic map) and radiation (a model anchored to MSL/RAD). It puts safety first: routes avoid steep terrain, and users can see the estimated dose and temperature along each route. We also include real photos and videos from NASA missions at the sites, so users can see what each place looks like.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Terrain, imagery, radiation and temperature usually live in separate tools. ARES puts them in one view so a crew can compare options before leaving the habitat. We use Gale as a human-scale case (a single-sol walk) and Tharsis for long-range traverse planning and choosing EVA sites. Our goal is to show how data from several NASA missions can become a decision tool, and to be a starting point for higher-resolution local planning.

A WALKTHROUGH: HOW A CREW WOULD USE ARES

  1. Choose a region and fly over the terrain in 3D or switch to the 2D map.
  2. Pick a start and a destination from the site list, or use a preset route.
  3. Set the season and the departure time (local mean solar time).
  4. Press “Compute routes” and compare the three options, using distance, maximum slope, estimated dose and temperature range.
  5. Check the elevation profile and the EVA window at the start point.
  6. Run the Marswalk to follow a simulated astronaut along the route, including pauses when walking is not allowed.

RESULTS

Case 1: Bradbury Landing → Curiosity’s latest position (Gale, Ls 90°, depart 09:00)

Curiosity’s actual recorded path is 38.3 km, because it stopped for science and did not drive directly. Sampling that real path on our 463 m grid gives a median slope of 2.3° and a maximum of 8.2° (69 samples), which is why we treat 8° as a reference for “steep”.

Case 2: Tharsis

At Pavonis in northern summer, EVA windows are 08:34–10:44 and 13:17–17:41 local time.

Validation

Real-world check (Curiosity). We compared ARES against a route that exists: Curiosity’s recorded traverse (38.3 km), sampled on our 463 m Gale grid at 69 points. It gives a median slope of 2.3° and a maximum of 8.2°. That is why ARES treats 8° as its reference for “steep”, and why the safest profile (max 4.4° Bradbury → Curiosity) stays well under it.

Data integrity. Our HD Tharsis inset came from a NASA Mars Trek OBJ export with no georeference. We recovered its position by correlating it with MOLA (r = 0.9999, median residual 1.2 m) and found it is MOLA resampled, not new topography. We say so in the app instead of presenting it as extra detail.

Resolution sensitivity. The same route on a finer grid gets steeper: Pavonis → Noctis Labyrinthus goes from 17.3° max slope (1/16°) to 21.9° (HD), and the safest Arsia → Noctis detour grows from 1,196 km to 1,314 km. Resolution changes the answer, so every route carries its grid.

Radiation anchor. The dose model is tied to the MSL/RAD measurement at Gale (0.64 ± 0.12 mSv/day, Hassler et al. 2014) and scaled with altitude using the published atmospheric column. The temperature model uses Mars Climate Database v6.2, with Curiosity REMS ground temperatures (≈173–289 K, Martínez et al. 2017) as the measured reference.

TOOLS

React, Vite, Three.js, OpenLayers, JavaScript (A* in a Web Worker) and Python (NumPy, Pillow). Data: NASA Mars Trek, MGS MOLA, Viking, CTX, THEMIS, MSL/RAD, Curiosity’s traverse (NASA/JPL MMGIS), NASA Photojournal and the Mars Climate Database.
